Last week, we looked at how dehydration puts your kidneys at risk. This week, the question is practical: How can you stay hydrated in this heat? With temperatures high across Nigeria, and climate patterns such as El Niño making hot spells worse, hydration matters more than ever. The World Health Organization warns that extreme heat can cause heat exhaustion and heat stroke, and that fluids lost through sweat must be replaced. Yet many of us reach for whatever is coldest and sweetest.
Did you know that not every drink helps equally?
Water is the best choice. It hydrates, it is cheap and it contains no sugar. Soft drinks, energy drinks and packaged juices contain some water, so they do add some fluid. But they carry a lot of sugar, which adds to the risk of weight gain and diabetes.
For people whose blood sugar runs very high, such as those with uncontrolled diabetes, excess sugar spills into the urine and pulls water with it, causing even more fluid loss. Alcohol makes you pass more urine, so it works against hydration and is best avoided on hot days. Tea and coffee have a mild diuretic effect, but moderate amounts still count toward your daily fluids.
How much should you drink?
Needs vary with body size, activity and weather. For most healthy adults, a general guide is about 1.5 to 3 litres of fluids a day, and more when it is hot or you work outdoors or exercise. Some of your fluid also comes from food. The exception to this is if your doctor has limited your fluids, for example because of a kidney, heart or liver disease. In that case, follow their advice.
Water is not the whole story
When you sweat heavily, you lose salts such as sodium along with water. For most people, normal meals replace them. But if you sweat for hours, for example during outdoor labour or sport, and drink very large amounts of plain water at one go, the sodium in your blood can become too diluted.
This rare condition called hyponatremia, causes headache, nausea, confusion and muscle cramps. So drink steadily through the day rather than gulping huge volumes at once, and eat regular meals. If you have vomiting or diarrhoea, oral rehydration salts (ORS), sold in pharmacies, are the right choice to hydrate.
Local options that help
* Water-rich fruits and vegetables: watermelon, oranges, pineapple, cucumber, tomatoes and garden eggs add fluid along with vitamins and minerals. * Coconut water: it contains potassium and other minerals and is refreshing,
* Zobo: Healthy zobo drinks with ginger and cloves can be a good choice if there is little or no sugar added. Another point to note is that hibiscus can lower blood pressure, so if you take blood pressure medication, check with your doctor.

Know the warning signs
Dizziness, headache, dark urine and unusual tiredness can be early signs that you need to rehydrate but confusion, fainting, very hot skin or a very high body temperature may mean heat stroke, which is an emergency. Get to a hospital immediately. Make hydration a daily habit, not a last-minute action. Keep water within reach, sip through the day, and do not wait until you are very thirsty.
